doc.title: Longineu Parsons interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, February 17, 2026

title: Writing long-form pieces and motivic development
summary: Rowe and Parsons compare how slowly notated music grows; Parsons needs long stretches of time and works with motivic development.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: Well you set quite a role model for your son, who sort of initiated this, and you pushed through.

Well done. I was wondering if you experience what I did once. We’re used to writing jazz tunes, and the model is write a head, improvise on the form, and then play the head again. And I was struck by when I listened to the recording of “Mr. P.C.” by John Coltrane originally and I timed the melody and his melody took 11 seconds. And the recording is 7 minutes long. So when I try to write classical music, what I will call “classical,” I was struck by how long you work on something and you play it back and like wow, I have one minute so far, because everything has to be notated you know, it’s like where is this going? I got one minute and it took me a week.
It can be that way. Yeah. So I don't know if I understand what you’re asking me.

I’m not asking a question, it’s really an observation, and I wondered if you had that experience of working on an ensemble piece or whatever, and thinking this is going really well but it’s still very short.

Mm hmm. Yeah well to me it’s always like that. That it takes quite a while for everything. But what I have found is that if I can have like a real lot of time to be devoted to the one thing then it gets faster as it goes. But to try to put in an hour or two here and there, I mean for me that first two hours is the warm up. That’s to get the mind ready to get where I was. But if I’m writing classical, I’m big into motific development. You know? So I’m into taking a little piece of this and seeing and doing all kinds of things with it.
